sentences.text: The genus Tarbosaurus contains only one recognized species, Tarbosaurus bataar, known from fragmentary remains in China and more complete fossils from Mongolia.
Its skull reached approximately 1.35 meters in length, making it larger than all other tyrannosaurids except Tyrannosaurus, while its arms were the smallest relative to body size among the group.
Fully developed adults measured between 10 and 12 meters long, stood 3 meters high at the hips, and weighed up to 4.5 tons, with jaws lined by between 58 and 64 teeth.
A complete skeleton returned to Mongolia in 2013 was temporarily displayed on Sukhbaatar Square in the capital city of Ulaanbaatar.
Footprints found at the Nemegt locality preserve skin impressions similar to those on the famous Bugiin Tsav skeleton, with one print measuring 61 centimeters in length.
Skin impressions from a large specimen discovered at Bugiin Tsav were unfortunately destroyed by poachers before they could be studied in detail.
Scientists have speculated that the animal's throat pouch might have been brightly colored and inflated for display purposes, resembling the pouch of a frigatebird.
A joint Soviet-Mongolian expedition first uncovered a large theropod skull and vertebrae in the Gobi Desert in 1946.
In 1979, Dong Zhiming described teeth, a dorsal vertebra, and fragmentary foot bones from South China that he tentatively assigned to Tarbosaurus.
A juvenile specimen with a skull measuring 290 millimeters was discovered in 2006 and formally described in 2011.
As an apex predator, Tarbosaurus hunted large dinosaurs such as the hadrosaurid Saurolophus and the sauropod Nemegtosaurus.
A 2005 study estimated its bite force at 8,000 to 10,000 pounds per square inch, while stress fractures in fossils suggest an active predation-based diet rather than scavenging.

Analysis of sclerotic rings suggests the juvenile may have been a crepuscular or nocturnal hunter, supported by large olfactory bulbs indicating a keen sense of smell but limited visual processing capabilities.
The lower jaw featured a unique locking mechanism formed by a ridge on the angular bone articulating with the dentary.
Most modern paleontologists recognize only Tarbosaurus bataar, though Shanshanosaurus huoyanshanensis is provisionally accepted as a synonym by subsequent authors.
The genus belongs to the theropod subfamily Tyrannosaurinae within the family Tyrannosauridae.
U-Pb dating suggests Tarbosaurus lived before 66.7 ± 2.5 million years ago during the Maastrichtian age, with estimates ranging from 70.6 to 68.5 million years ago.
It inhabited a humid floodplain environment dominated by deserts, forests, and plains criss-crossed by river channels.
About one-quarter of all fossils collected from the Nemegt Formation belong to this species.
Some experts consider Tarbosaurus bataar to be an Asian representative of Tyrannosaurus, which would render the genus Tarbosaurus redundant.
Currie speculated that Alioramus might be a juvenile Tarbosaurus, but noted that its high tooth count and snout crests suggested otherwise.
It is debated whether scattered tyrannosaurid remains from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia belong to Tarbosaurus, as some researchers consider them dubious or foreign passing taxa.
